name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q01 - VSEPR molecular geometries without lone pairs

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with their molecular geometries given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Geometry)
1. \(\mathrm{BeCl}_{2}\)A. Octahedral
2. \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\)B. Linear
3. \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\)C. Tetrahedral
4. \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\)D. Trigonal planar

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to VSEPR theory, when the central atom of a molecule has no lone pairs, its molecular geometry is identical to the spatial arrangement of its bonding electron pairs that minimizes repulsion.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{BeCl}_{2}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{2}\) type) has \(2\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs around beryllium, giving a linear geometry (\(180^{\circ}\)).
- \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{3}\) type) has \(3\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs around boron, giving a trigonal planar geometry (\(120^{\circ}\)).
- \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{4}\) type) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs around carbon, giving a tetrahedral geometry (\(109.5^{\circ}\)).
- \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{6}\) type) has \(6\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs around sulphur, giving an octahedral geometry (\(90^{\circ}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{BeCl}_{2} \rightarrow\) Linear, \(\mathrm{BF}_{3} \rightarrow\) Trigonal planar, \(\mathrm{CH}_{4} \rightarrow\) Tetrahedral, and \(\mathrm{SF}_{6} \rightarrow\) Octahedral.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q02 - Hybridisation of central atoms in simple molecules

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with the hybridisation of their central atom given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Hybridisation)
1. \(\mathrm{BeCl}_{2}\)A. \(sp^{3}\)
2. \(\mathrm{BCl}_{3}\)B. \(sp^{3}d\)
3. \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\)C. \(sp\)
4. \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\)D. \(sp^{2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The number of hybrid orbitals formed equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed, which corresponds to the number of \(\sigma\) bonds and lone pairs around the central atom.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- In \(\mathrm{BeCl}_{2}\), beryllium mixes one \(2s\) and one \(2p\) orbital to form two \(sp\) hybrid orbitals.
- In \(\mathrm{BCl}_{3}\), boron mixes one \(2s\) and two \(2p\) orbitals to form three \(sp^{2}\) hybrid orbitals.
- In \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\), carbon mixes one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals to form four \(sp^{3}\) hybrid orbitals.
- In \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\), phosphorus mixes one \(3s\), three \(3p\), and one \(3d\) orbital to form five \(sp^{3}d\) hybrid orbitals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{BeCl}_{2} \rightarrow sp\), \(\mathrm{BCl}_{3} \rightarrow sp^{2}\), \(\mathrm{CH}_{4} \rightarrow sp^{3}\), and \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5} \rightarrow sp^{3}d\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q03 - Bond order of homonuclear diatomic molecules

questiontext.text:
Match the diatomic species given in List-I with their bond orders given in List-II.

List-I (Species)List-II (Bond Order)
1. \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\)A. \(2\)
2. \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\)B. \(0\)
3. \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\)C. \(3\)
4. \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\)D. \(1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to molecular orbital theory, bond order is given by \(\frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\), where \(N_{b}\) and \(N_{a}\) are the numbers of electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals, respectively.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) has configuration \((\sigma 1s)^{2}\): bond order \(= \frac{1}{2}(2 - 0) = 1\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) has \(10\) bonding and \(6\) antibonding electrons: bond order \(= \frac{1}{2}(10 - 6) = 2\).
- \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) has \(10\) bonding and \(4\) antibonding electrons: bond order \(= \frac{1}{2}(10 - 4) = 3\).
- \(\mathrm{He}_{2}\) has configuration \((\sigma 1s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 1s)^{2}\): bond order \(= \frac{1}{2}(2 - 2) = 0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{H}_{2} \rightarrow 1\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\), \(\mathrm{N}_{2} \rightarrow 3\), and \(\mathrm{He}_{2} \rightarrow 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q04 - Molecular shapes with lone pairs on central atom

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with their VSEPR shapes given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Shape)
1. \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\)A. T-shape
2. \(\mathrm{SF}_{4}\)B. Square planar
3. \(\mathrm{ClF}_{3}\)C. Trigonal pyramidal
4. \(\mathrm{XeF}_{4}\)D. See-saw

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In VSEPR theory, molecular shape is determined by the positions of the bonded atoms after accounting for the spatial arrangement of both bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{3}\mathrm{E}\) type) has \(3\) bond pairs and \(1\) lone pair in a tetrahedral arrangement, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape.
- \(\mathrm{SF}_{4}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{4}\mathrm{E}\) type) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(1\) equatorial lone pair in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, giving a see-saw shape.
- \(\mathrm{ClF}_{3}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{3}\mathrm{E}_{2}\) type) has \(3\) bond pairs and \(2\) equatorial lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, giving a T-shape.
- \(\mathrm{XeF}_{4}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{4}\mathrm{E}_{2}\) type) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(2\) trans lone pairs in an octahedral arrangement, giving a square planar shape.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow\) Trigonal pyramidal, \(\mathrm{SF}_{4} \rightarrow\) See-saw, \(\mathrm{ClF}_{3} \rightarrow\) T-shape, and \(\mathrm{XeF}_{4} \rightarrow\) Square planar.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q05 - Dipole moments of common covalent molecules

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with their experimental dipole moments (\(\mu\)) given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Dipole Moment)
1. \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\)A. \(0\ \mathrm{D}\)
2. \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\)B. \(1.85\ \mathrm{D}\)
3. \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\)C. \(0.23\ \mathrm{D}\)
4. \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\)D. \(1.47\ \mathrm{D}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The net dipole moment of a polyatomic molecule is the vector sum of its individual bond dipoles and any lone-pair orbital dipoles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) has a bent shape (\(104.5^{\circ}\)) with two polar \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bonds and two lone pairs, giving a high dipole moment of \(1.85\ \mathrm{D}\).
- \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) has a trigonal pyramidal shape where the lone-pair dipole reinforces the three \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond dipoles, giving \(1.47\ \mathrm{D}\).
- \(\mathrm{NF}_{3}\) also has a trigonal pyramidal shape, but the lone-pair dipole opposes the resultant of the three \(\mathrm{N-F}\) bond dipoles, reducing the net dipole moment to \(0.23\ \mathrm{D}\).
- \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) is a symmetrical trigonal planar molecule (\(120^{\circ}\)) where the three \(\mathrm{B-F}\) bond dipoles cancel completely, giving \(0\ \mathrm{D}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 1.85\ \mathrm{D}\), \(\mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow 1.47\ \mathrm{D}\), \(\mathrm{NF}_{3} \rightarrow 0.23\ \mathrm{D}\), and \(\mathrm{BF}_{3} \rightarrow 0\ \mathrm{D}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q06 - Classification of molecules under the octet rule

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with their valence electron classification given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Octet Classification)
1. \(\mathrm{BeH}_{2}\)A. Expanded octet
2. \(\mathrm{NO}\)B. Obeys octet rule
3. \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\)C. Incomplete octet
4. \(\mathrm{SCl}_{2}\)D. Odd-electron molecule

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The octet rule states that atoms tend to achieve eight electrons in their valence shell. Exceptions include incomplete octets (fewer than \(8\) electrons), odd-electron molecules, and expanded octets (more than \(8\) electrons).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- In \(\mathrm{BeH}_{2}\), beryllium has only \(2\) valence electrons and forms \(2\) covalent bonds, giving \(4\) electrons around \(\mathrm{Be}\) (incomplete octet).
- \(\mathrm{NO}\) has \(5 + 6 = 11\) valence electrons, making it an odd-electron molecule.
- In \(\mathrm{SF}_{6}\), sulphur forms \(6\) covalent bonds, giving \(12\) electrons around \(\mathrm{S}\) (expanded octet).
- In \(\mathrm{SCl}_{2}\), sulphur forms \(2\) single bonds and retains \(2\) lone pairs, giving \(8\) electrons around \(\mathrm{S}\) (obeys octet rule).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{BeH}_{2} \rightarrow\) Incomplete octet, \(\mathrm{NO} \rightarrow\) Odd-electron molecule, \(\mathrm{SF}_{6} \rightarrow\) Expanded octet, and \(\mathrm{SCl}_{2} \rightarrow\) Obeys octet rule.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q07 - Hybridisation schemes involving d orbitals

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules or complex ions given in List-I with their hybridisation and shape given in List-II.

List-I (Species)List-II (Hybridisation & Shape)
1. \([\mathrm{Ni(CN)}_{4}]^{2-}\)A. \(sp^{3}d\), Trigonal bipyramidal
2. \(\mathrm{BrF}_{5}\)B. \(dsp^{2}\), Square planar
3. \([\mathrm{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}\)C. \(d^{2}sp^{3}\), Octahedral
4. \(\mathrm{PF}_{5}\)D. \(sp^{3}d^{2}\), Square pyramidal

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elements and ions with available \(d\) orbitals of comparable energy to \(s\) and \(p\) orbitals can undergo \(dsp^{2}\), \(sp^{3}d\), \(sp^{3}d^{2}\), or \(d^{2}sp^{3}\) hybridisation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \([\mathrm{Ni(CN)}_{4}]^{2-}\) uses one inner \(d\), one \(s\), and two \(p\) orbitals (\(dsp^{2}\)), adopting a square planar shape.
- \(\mathrm{BrF}_{5}\) uses one \(s\), three \(p\), and two \(d\) orbitals (\(sp^{3}d^{2}\)) with \(5\) bond pairs and \(1\) lone pair, adopting a square pyramidal shape.
- \([\mathrm{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+}\) uses two inner \(d\), one \(s\), and three \(p\) orbitals (\(d^{2}sp^{3}\)), adopting an octahedral shape.
- \(\mathrm{PF}_{5}\) uses one \(s\), three \(p\), and one \(d\) orbital (\(sp^{3}d\)), adopting a trigonal bipyramidal shape.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \([\mathrm{Ni(CN)}_{4}]^{2-} \rightarrow dsp^{2}\) (Square planar), \(\mathrm{BrF}_{5} \rightarrow sp^{3}d^{2}\) (Square pyramidal), \([\mathrm{Co(NH}_{3})_{6}]^{3+} \rightarrow d^{2}sp^{3}\) (Octahedral), and \(\mathrm{PF}_{5} \rightarrow sp^{3}d\) (Trigonal bipyramidal).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q08 - Average covalent bond lengths for carbon and oxygen bonds

questiontext.text:
Match the covalent bond types given in List-I with their average bond lengths given in List-II.

List-I (Bond Type)List-II (Bond Length)
1. \(\mathrm{C-C}\)A. \(96\ \mathrm{pm}\)
2. \(\mathrm{C=C}\)B. \(133\ \mathrm{pm}\)
3. \(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\)C. \(120\ \mathrm{pm}\)
4. \(\mathrm{O-H}\)D. \(154\ \mathrm{pm}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a given pair of atoms, bond length decreases as bond order (multiplicity) increases from a single bond to a double bond to a triple bond. Bonds involving the very small hydrogen atom are even shorter.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Bond Type
- The carbon–carbon single bond (\(\mathrm{C-C}\)) has the longest length among carbon–carbon bonds at \(154\ \mathrm{pm}\).
- The carbon–carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{C=C}\)) is shorter at \(133\ \mathrm{pm}\).
- The carbon–carbon triple bond (\(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\)) is shorter still at \(120\ \mathrm{pm}\).
- The \(\mathrm{O-H}\) single bond involves small \(\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms and has an average length of \(96\ \mathrm{pm}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{C-C} \rightarrow 154\ \mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{C=C} \rightarrow 133\ \mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{C\equiv C} \rightarrow 120\ \mathrm{pm}\), and \(\mathrm{O-H} \rightarrow 96\ \mathrm{pm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q09 - Magnetic behaviour and valence molecular orbitals of diatomic molecules

questiontext.text:
Match the homonuclear diatomic molecules given in List-I with their magnetic properties and valence orbital occupancy given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Property)
1. \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\)A. Paramagnetic with \(2\) unpaired electrons in \(\pi 2p\)
2. \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\)B. Diamagnetic with bond order \(1\)
3. \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\)C. Paramagnetic with \(2\) unpaired electrons in \(\pi^{*} 2p\)
4. \(\mathrm{Li}_{2}\)D. Diamagnetic with bond order \(2\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For \(\mathrm{Li}_{2}\), \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\), and \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\), \((\pi 2p_{x} = \pi 2p_{y})\) is lower in energy than \(\sigma 2p_{z}\), whereas for \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\), \(\sigma 2p_{z}\) is lower than \((\pi 2p_{x} = \pi 2p_{y})\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) (\(10\) electrons) has \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}(\pi 2p_{x}^{1} = \pi 2p_{y}^{1})\), so it is paramagnetic with \(2\) unpaired electrons in \(\pi 2p\).
- \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) (\(12\) electrons) has \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}(\pi 2p_{x}^{2} = \pi 2p_{y}^{2})\), so it is diamagnetic with bond order \(2\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) (\(16\) electrons) has \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^{2}(\sigma^{*} 2s)^{2}(\sigma 2p_{z})^{2}(\pi 2p_{x}^{2} = \pi 2p_{y}^{2})(\pi^{*} 2p_{x}^{1} = \pi^{*} 2p_{y}^{1})\), so it is paramagnetic with \(2\) unpaired electrons in \(\pi^{*} 2p\).
- \(\mathrm{Li}_{2}\) (\(6\) electrons) has \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^{2}\), so it is diamagnetic with bond order \(1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{B}_{2} \rightarrow\) Paramagnetic with \(2\) unpaired electrons in \(\pi 2p\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2} \rightarrow\) Diamagnetic with bond order \(2\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow\) Paramagnetic with \(2\) unpaired electrons in \(\pi^{*} 2p\), and \(\mathrm{Li}_{2} \rightarrow\) Diamagnetic with bond order \(1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q10 - Number of sigma and pi bonds in covalent molecules

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with the total number of \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) bonds present in each molecule given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Number of \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) Bonds)
1. \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{6}\)A. \(3\sigma,\ 2\pi\)
2. \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{4}\)B. \(2\sigma,\ 2\pi\)
3. \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{2}\)C. \(7\sigma,\ 0\pi\)
4. \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\)D. \(5\sigma,\ 1\pi\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Every single covalent bond is a \(\sigma\) bond. A double bond consists of \(1\sigma\) and \(1\pi\) bond, and a triple bond consists of \(1\sigma\) and \(2\pi\) bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{6}\) (\(\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{C-CH}_{3}\)) has one \(\mathrm{C-C}\) single bond and six \(\mathrm{C-H}\) single bonds, giving \(7\sigma\) and \(0\pi\) bonds.
- \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{4}\) (\(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{C=CH}_{2}\)) has one \(\mathrm{C=C}\) double bond (\(1\sigma, 1\pi\)) and four \(\mathrm{C-H}\) single bonds (\(4\sigma\)), giving \(5\sigma\) and \(1\pi\) bonds.
- \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{2}\) (\(\mathrm{HC\equiv CH}\)) has one \(\mathrm{C\equiv C}\) triple bond (\(1\sigma, 2\pi\)) and two \(\mathrm{C-H}\) single bonds (\(2\sigma\)), giving \(3\sigma\) and \(2\pi\) bonds.
- \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) (\(\mathrm{O=C=O}\)) has two \(\mathrm{C=O}\) double bonds, giving \(2\sigma\) and \(2\pi\) bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{6} \rightarrow 7\sigma,\ 0\pi\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{4} \rightarrow 5\sigma,\ 1\pi\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{2} \rightarrow 3\sigma,\ 2\pi\), and \(\mathrm{CO}_{2} \rightarrow 2\sigma,\ 2\pi\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q11 - Bond angles in molecules with and without lone pairs

questiontext.text:
Match the molecules given in List-I with their bond angles given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Bond Angle)
1. \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\)A. \(104.5^{\circ}\)
2. \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\)B. \(119.5^{\circ}\)
3. \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\)C. \(109.5^{\circ}\)
4. \(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\)D. \(107^{\circ}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In VSEPR theory, lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs and exert greater repulsion (\(\mathrm{lp-lp} > \mathrm{lp-bp} > \mathrm{bp-bp}\)), compressing the bond angle below the ideal geometry value.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{CH}_{4}\) has \(4\) bond pairs and \(0\) lone pairs, retaining the ideal tetrahedral angle of \(109.5^{\circ}\).
- \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) has \(3\) bond pairs and \(1\) lone pair, reducing the \(\mathrm{H-N-H}\) angle from \(109.5^{\circ}\) to \(107^{\circ}\).
- \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}\) has \(2\) bond pairs and \(2\) lone pairs, further reducing the \(\mathrm{H-O-H}\) angle to \(104.5^{\circ}\).
- \(\mathrm{SO}_{2}\) (\(\mathrm{AB}_{2}\mathrm{E}\) type) has a trigonal planar electron-pair arrangement with \(1\) lone pair, reducing the \(\mathrm{O-S-O}\) angle from \(120^{\circ}\) to \(119.5^{\circ}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{CH}_{4} \rightarrow 109.5^{\circ}\), \(\mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow 107^{\circ}\), \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 104.5^{\circ}\), and \(\mathrm{SO}_{2} \rightarrow 119.5^{\circ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q12 - Bond orders of dioxygen molecule and its ions

questiontext.text:
Match the oxygen species given in List-I with their bond orders given in List-II.

List-I (Species)List-II (Bond Order)
1. \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\)A. \(1.0\)
2. \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\)B. \(2.0\)
3. \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\)C. \(2.5\)
4. \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\)D. \(1.5\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bond order is calculated as \(\frac{1}{2}(N_{b} - N_{a})\). Adding electrons to antibonding \(\pi^{*} 2p\) orbitals decreases the bond order, while removing electrons from \(\pi^{*} 2p\) increases it.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}\) (\(16\) electrons) has \(N_{b} = 10\) and \(N_{a} = 6\), so \(\mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 6) = 2.0\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+}\) (\(15\) electrons) has one fewer antibonding electron (\(N_{a} = 5\)), so \(\mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 5) = 2.5\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}\) (\(17\) electrons, superoxide) has one extra antibonding electron (\(N_{a} = 7\)), so \(\mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 7) = 1.5\).
- \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-}\) (\(18\) electrons, peroxide) has two extra antibonding electrons (\(N_{a} = 8\)), so \(\mathrm{BO} = \frac{1}{2}(10 - 8) = 1.0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{+} \rightarrow 2.5\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2.0\), \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-} \rightarrow 1.5\), and \(\mathrm{O}_{2}^{2-} \rightarrow 1.0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q13 - Hybridisation changes in Lewis acid-base reactions

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical processes or species given in List-I with the corresponding hybridisation state or change given in List-II.

List-I (Process / Species)List-II (Hybridisation State / Change)
1. \(\mathrm{AlCl}_{3} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{AlCl}_{4}^{-}\)A. \(sp^{2} \rightarrow sp^{3}\) on \(\mathrm{Al}\)
2. \(\mathrm{BF}_{3} + \mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (at \(\mathrm{N}\))B. \(sp^{3}\) remains \(sp^{3}\) on \(\mathrm{N}\)
3. \(\mathrm{BF}_{3} + \mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (at \(\mathrm{B}\))C. \(sp^{2} \rightarrow sp^{3}\) on \(\mathrm{B}\)
4. \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\)D. \(sp^{3}d\) on \(\mathrm{P}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When a trigonal planar molecule (\(sp^{2}\) hybridised) accepts an electron pair to form a fourth \(\sigma\) bond, its central atom rehybridises to tetrahedral (\(sp^{3}\)). If the donor atom already has four electron pairs (\(3\sigma + 1\ \mathrm{lp}\)), its hybridisation remains \(sp^{3}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Case
- In \(\mathrm{AlCl}_{3} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{AlCl}_{4}^{-}\), \(\mathrm{Al}\) goes from \(3\) bond pairs (\(sp^{2}\)) to \(4\) bond pairs (\(sp^{3}\)).
- In \(\mathrm{BF}_{3} + \mathrm{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\), the \(\mathrm{N}\) atom in \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) has \(3\sigma\) bonds and \(1\) lone pair (\(sp^{3}\)); upon donating its lone pair to \(\mathrm{B}\), it still has \(4\sigma\) bonds, so its hybridisation remains \(sp^{3}\).
- In the same adduct formation, \(\mathrm{B}\) goes from \(3\) bond pairs in \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) (\(sp^{2}\)) to \(4\) bond pairs (\(sp^{3}\)).
- In \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\), phosphorus forms \(5\sigma\) bonds using \(sp^{3}d\) hybridisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{AlCl}_{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{AlCl}_{4}^{-}\) (\(sp^{2} \rightarrow sp^{3}\) on \(\mathrm{Al}\)), \(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) in \(\mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (\(sp^{3}\) remains \(sp^{3}\) on \(\mathrm{N}\)), \(\mathrm{BF}_{3}\) in \(\mathrm{F}_{3}\mathrm{B}\cdot\mathrm{NH}_{3}\) (\(sp^{2} \rightarrow sp^{3}\) on \(\mathrm{B}\)), and \(\mathrm{PCl}_{5}\) (\(sp^{3}d\) on \(\mathrm{P}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q14 - Bond energy and bond length of second-row diatomic molecules

questiontext.text:
Match the homonuclear diatomic molecules given in List-I with their bond energy and bond length values given in List-II.

List-I (Molecule)List-II (Bond Energy, Bond Length)
1. \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\)A. \(945\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 110\ \mathrm{pm}\)
2. \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\)B. \(159\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 143\ \mathrm{pm}\)
3. \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\)C. \(290\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 159\ \mathrm{pm}\)
4. \(\mathrm{F}_{2}\)D. \(620\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 131\ \mathrm{pm}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As bond order increases, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases. Comparing molecules of the same bond order, larger atomic radius or lone-pair repulsion weakens and lengthens the bond.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
- \(\mathrm{N}_{2}\) has the highest bond order (\(3\)), giving the highest bond energy (\(945\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and shortest bond length (\(110\ \mathrm{pm}\)).
- \(\mathrm{C}_{2}\) has bond order \(2\), with an intermediate bond energy (\(620\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and bond length (\(131\ \mathrm{pm}\)).
- \(\mathrm{B}_{2}\) has bond order \(1\) with larger boron atoms, giving a bond energy of \(290\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) and bond length of \(159\ \mathrm{pm}\).
- \(\mathrm{F}_{2}\) has bond order \(1\) with a weaker single bond (\(159\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and bond length of \(143\ \mathrm{pm}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(\mathrm{B}_{2} \rightarrow 290\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 159\ \mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{C}_{2} \rightarrow 620\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 131\ \mathrm{pm}\), \(\mathrm{N}_{2} \rightarrow 945\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 110\ \mathrm{pm}\), and \(\mathrm{F}_{2} \rightarrow 159\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}},\ 143\ \mathrm{pm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q15 - Formal charges and resonance bond length in ozone

questiontext.text:
Match the features of the ozone (\(\mathrm{O}_{3}\)) molecule given in List-I with their values given in List-II.

List-I (Feature of \(\mathrm{O}_{3}\))List-II (Value)
1. Formal charge on central \(\mathrm{O}\) atomA. \(0\)
2. Formal charge on single-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\) atomB. \(128\ \mathrm{pm}\)
3. Formal charge on double-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\) atomC. \(+1\)
4. Experimental \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bond length in resonance hybridD. \(-1\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Formal charge is calculated as \(\mathrm{F.C.} = V - L - \frac{1}{2}B\). In a resonance hybrid, the actual bond length is intermediate between the single-bond and double-bond lengths of the canonical forms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Feature
- Central \(\mathrm{O}\) atom has \(1\) lone pair (\(L = 2\)) and \(3\) bonds (\(B = 6\)): \(\mathrm{F.C.} = 6 - 2 - \frac{1}{2}(6) = +1\).
- Single-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\) atom has \(3\) lone pairs (\(L = 6\)) and \(1\) bond (\(B = 2\)): \(\mathrm{F.C.} = 6 - 6 - \frac{1}{2}(2) = -1\).
- Double-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O}\) atom has \(2\) lone pairs (\(L = 4\)) and \(2\) bonds (\(B = 4\)): \(\mathrm{F.C.} = 6 - 4 - \frac{1}{2}(4) = 0\).
- Experimentally, both \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bonds in the \(\mathrm{O}_{3}\) resonance hybrid are equal at \(128\ \mathrm{pm}\) (intermediate between \(148\ \mathrm{pm}\) and \(121\ \mathrm{pm}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are central \(\mathrm{O} \rightarrow +1\), single-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O} \rightarrow -1\), double-bonded terminal \(\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 0\), and experimental \(\mathrm{O-O}\) bond length \(\rightarrow 128\ \mathrm{pm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q16 - Types of orbital overlap along the x-internuclear axis

questiontext.text:
Considering the \(x\)-axis as the internuclear axis, match the pairs of approaching half-filled atomic orbitals given in List-I with the type of overlap/bond formed given in List-II.

List-I (Atomic Orbitals)List-II (Overlap / Bond Type)
1. \(1s\) and \(1s\)A. Forms \(\pi\) bond (sidewise overlap)
2. \(1s\) and \(2p_{x}\)B. Zero overlap (no bond formed)
3. \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{y}\)C. Forms \(\sigma\) bond (\(s-s\) axial overlap)
4. \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{z}\)D. Forms \(\sigma\) bond (\(s-p\) axial overlap)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
With the \(x\)-axis as the internuclear axis, head-on (axial) overlap along the \(x\)-axis produces \(\sigma\) bonds, whereas sidewise overlap of parallel \(p\) orbitals perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis produces \(\pi\) bonds. Orbitals of incompatible symmetry give zero overlap.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
- \(1s\) and \(1s\) are spherically symmetrical and overlap axially along the \(x\)-axis to form a \(\sigma\) bond (\(s-s\) axial overlap).
- \(1s\) and \(2p_{x}\) overlap head-on along the \(x\)-axis to form a \(\sigma\) bond (\(s-p\) axial overlap).
- \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{y}\) have parallel axes perpendicular to the \(x\)-internuclear axis, so they overlap sidewise to form a \(\pi\) bond.
- \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{z}\) are mutually perpendicular and have different symmetries about the internuclear axis, resulting in zero overlap.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are \(1s\) and \(1s \rightarrow \sigma\) bond (\(s-s\) axial overlap), \(1s\) and \(2p_{x} \rightarrow \sigma\) bond (\(s-p\) axial overlap), \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{y} \rightarrow \pi\) bond (sidewise overlap), and \(2p_{y}\) and \(2p_{z} \rightarrow\) Zero overlap.
